strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning for humanoid whole-body control.

PvP is simple and potentially useful: it applies a shared encoder and SimSiam-style objective to full privileged states and zero-masked, deployable proprioceptive states, avoiding manually designed augmentation pairs.

The evaluation covers two distinct control settings—velocity tracking and imitation of 20 motion sequences—and PvP shows a large convergence improvement on velocity tracking and the strongest final normalized score on imitation.

The comparison includes reconstruction-, dynamics-, and similarity-based representation-learning baselines under a common PPO architecture. Ablations on update interval, data fraction, and policy-versus-value encoder placement provide useful practical observations.

Sim2Sim and real-hardware demonstrations increase the practical relevance, while the proposed modular SRL4Humanoid framework could be a useful community resource if released with the claimed implementations and configurations.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are insufficiently quantified. Most results are normalized learning curves with no definition of the normalization, raw returns, sample counts at performance thresholds, numerical tables, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The number of random seeds is not reported, despite showing mean and standard-deviation bands. Consequently, claims of significant improvement and sample efficiency cannot be reliably assessed.

The real-world evidence is qualitative: the paper provides images and refers to videos, but reports no number of trials, success rates, tracking errors, falls, robustness tests, or comparison against PPO and other baselines on hardware. It therefore does not support claims that PvP guarantees deployment reliability or improves real-world performance.

The computational-efficiency claim is unsupported in the manuscript. Section 5.2.5 reports neither wall-clock time, throughput, memory consumption, nor auxiliary-loss overhead, and instead refers to logs in a compute-reporting form. Running on one GPU does not establish minimal computational cost.

The method has important implementation ambiguities. Equations 2–4 describe the privileged state as containing the proprioceptive state and apply the same encoder to the full and masked vectors, whereas Tables 2–4 list differently structured privileged and proprioceptive inputs, including five-frame stacking only on one side. The paper does not clearly state which representation is fed to PPO during training or fully specify the padding, normalization, predictor architecture, and gradient interaction between PPO and PvP.

Novelty is modest: algorithmically, PvP is chiefly SimSiam applied to a privileged input and its zero-masked version. There is no ablation isolating whether the gain comes from cross-view representation learning, privileged-state regularization, ordinary feature masking, or auxiliary prediction of the small set of privileged variables. Comparisons to asymmetric actor-critic, teacher-student, privileged-information distillation, and reconstruction-based humanoid methods are limited or absent.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the framework claim. SRL-module architectures and optimizer settings are incomplete, domain-randomization and evaluation protocols are not specified, hyperparameter-search selection criteria and budgets are omitted, and the framework is described as open source without an accessible artifact in the manuscript.

Evaluation breadth is limited to one robot model, flat-ground velocity tracking, and one collection of motion clips. There are no held-out motions, terrain changes, perturbations, sensor noise studies, or morphology/domain shifts, so the claims of broad versatility, robustness, and generalization exceed the presented evidence.

There are several correctness and clarity issues: figures alternate between 31-DoF and 32-DoF task names; the SimSiam baseline equation omits the predictor, stop-gradient, and symmetric objective described in the original method; and the rationale about early low-quality data causing local optima is asserted without direct representation-level evidence. These inconsistencies further complicate interpretation and reproduction.

strengths: The core idea is simple and potentially useful: align privileged-state and masked proprioceptive representations with a SimSiam-style auxiliary objective so that the deployed policy can operate from proprioception alone.

The reported learning curves show a substantial and consistent-looking acceleration on velocity tracking and a smaller improvement on motion imitation relative to PPO and the implemented SRL baselines.
The paper studies several practically relevant design choices, including SRL update frequency, data proportion, and whether the auxiliary loss is attached to the policy or value encoder.
The manuscript is generally readable, provides reward and observation definitions in the supplement, and includes qualitative simulation-to-simulation and real-robot demonstrations.
weaknesses: The central comparison is materially confounded: PvP receives privileged variables, whereas the VAE, SPR, and ordinary SimSiam baselines operate on proprioception. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether the gain comes from the proposed cross-view objective or simply from supplying extra training-time information. Missing controls include privileged-information reconstruction/distillation, asymmetric teacher-student learning, and alternative alignment losses using the same privileged inputs.

The empirical evidence is insufficiently quantified. Results are mostly normalized curves whose normalization is not defined, with no tables of raw returns, tracking errors, success rates, samples needed to reach a threshold, or statistical tests. Although plots show means and standard deviations, the number of seeds is never reported. This makes claims of significant improvement and sample efficiency difficult to verify.

The real-world evidence is qualitative only. The paper reports no number of trials, command or motion coverage, tracking error, fall rate, robustness tests, comparison against PPO or other baselines, or failure analysis. Optimizing an action-smoothness reward in simulation does not by itself guarantee reliable real-world deployment, contrary to the manuscript's claim.

The contribution is technically incremental: PvP applies a standard SimSiam loss to a privileged input and its zero-masked version. The manuscript provides neither analysis explaining why this objective should outperform privileged-state prediction/distillation nor representation diagnostics demonstrating task relevance, retained privileged information, or absence of collapse.

Evaluation breadth is limited to two tasks on one embodiment: flat-ground velocity tracking and imitation of 20 motions. There is no test across terrains, disturbances, morphology changes, held-out motions, or another robot. This substantially weakens the claims that the method is broadly versatile and produces robust representations.

The computational-efficiency conclusion is unsupported. Running an auxiliary module on the GPU does not imply negligible overhead, yet the paper reports no wall-clock time, throughput, memory usage, or compute comparison. Referring to private compute-form logs is not a substitute for evidence in the manuscript.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the open-source-framework claim: no accessible code location is provided in the manuscript, and important details such as random-seed count, projection/predictor architectures, normalization, domain randomization, PD gains, termination conditions, precise update scheduling, and real-world deployment protocol are absent. The appendix's SimSiam equation also omits the predictor, stop-gradient, and symmetric objective used in the main method description.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. The assertions that early low-quality data causes representation learning to enter local optima, that interval 50 prevents this behavior, and that PvP learns compact task-relevant features are not supported by targeted measurements or ablations.

There are presentation inconsistencies, including alternating 31-DoF and 32-DoF task names and ambiguous notation for the interval indicator. These are correctable issues rather than the main basis for rejection, but they further hinder precise interpretation. strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: improving the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning for humanoid whole-body control.

PvP is simple and potentially useful: aligning privileged and deployable proprioceptive views through a shared encoder and stop-gradient objective can be integrated into an asymmetric actor-critic pipeline without requiring privileged inputs at deployment.
The evaluation covers two distinct tasks—velocity tracking and imitation of 20 motions—on a full-size 31-DoF humanoid, and includes qualitative MuJoCo and real-robot demonstrations.

The reported learning curves consistently favor PvP over PPO, VAE, SPR, and SimSiam, with especially large early-training gains for velocity tracking. The ablations on update interval, data proportion, and encoder placement provide useful practical observations.
The supplementary material reports observation components, rewards, network sizes, PPO settings, and baseline hyperparameter-search spaces, improving reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central sample-efficiency claim is not quantified rigorously. Results use normalized score versus percentage of training progress, without defining normalization, reporting environment steps to a target, area under the learning curve, or numerical confidence intervals. The number of random seeds is also omitted, so statements such as “significantly” improves performance are unsupported statistically.

The most relevant alternatives are missing. PvP is not compared with privileged-state regression, teacher-student distillation, concurrent teacher-student learning, or the cited humanoid-specific privileged/reconstruction approaches. Consequently, the experiments do not isolate whether the gain comes from the proposed Siamese objective or simply from injecting privileged supervision.

The stated SimSiam implementation is technically concerning: Appendix Eq. 12 omits SimSiam's predictor and stop-gradient asymmetry, whereas PvP explicitly includes both. If this equation reflects the implementation, the key baseline is misimplemented and the comparison is not fair; if it is only an exposition error, the implementation still needs clarification.

Real-world evidence is qualitative only. The manuscript provides image sequences and references videos but reports no number of trials, success rate, tracking error, perturbation tests, or baseline deployment comparison. Simulation action smoothness alone does not substantiate the claimed real-world reliability.

The computational-efficiency claim lacks evidence: there are no wall-clock times, throughput, memory use, or overhead measurements. Running the auxiliary loss on a GPU does not imply that it has no effect on training efficiency.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The predictor/projector architecture, SRL optimizer details, default update schedule, domain-randomization settings, seed count, score normalization, motion-data provenance, and quantitative deployment protocol are not specified. The claimed open-source framework is not accompanied by an accessible artifact in the manuscript.

Generality is demonstrated only on one robot and two closely related control settings, primarily on flat terrain. There is no evaluation under disturbances, terrain variation, or morphology changes, even though broad task versatility and robustness are emphasized.

The novelty is incremental: PvP largely applies a SimSiam-style consistency loss to privileged and zero-masked proprioceptive views. Without comparisons to direct privileged prediction/distillation or analyses of learned representations, it is difficult to establish that the proposed contrastive formulation is the source of the gains.

Presentation inconsistencies—including repeated “32dof” figure labels for a robot and tasks described as 31-DoF, the undefined normalized-score transformation, and referring to SimSiam as contrastive learning—reduce clarity but are secondary to the evidentiary concerns above.

strengths: PvP is simple, technically plausible, and easy to integrate: it applies a SimSiam-style objective between full privileged states and zero-masked proprioceptive views while retaining a proprioceptive policy for deployment.

The evaluation covers velocity tracking and motion imitation, with additional appendix experiments on rough terrain and a Unitree G1 platform. Comparisons include reconstruction-, dynamics-, and contrastive-learning baselines, plus teacher-student distillation.

The ablations examine update interval, training-data proportion, policy versus value encoder placement, and loss weight. They provide useful practical observations, including instability when regularizing the value encoder.
The appendix documents observations, rewards, network architectures, PPO settings, and baseline hyperparameter searches. The proposed SRL4Humanoid framework could be useful if released as claimed.
The learning curves consistently indicate that PvP improves convergence and often final reward, particularly on the principal LimX Oli tasks.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are inadequately quantified. Results are predominantly plots of normalized reward, with no numerical tables, definition of the normalization, number of random seeds, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or explicit sample-efficiency measures. Calling improvements “significant” is therefore unsupported.

The real-world evidence is qualitative: robot images and a reference to supplementary videos are provided, but there are no trial counts, success rates, tracking errors, robustness tests, deployment durations, or comparisons against PPO and other baselines. This does not substantiate claims of reliable real-world improvement.

The experimental protocol contains a consequential ambiguity. Section 4.2 states that the policy receives proprioception and the critic receives privileged state, yet Figures 13–15 distinguish standard “PPO” from “PPO (only Proprio.)” and report that the latter fails. The manuscript does not reconcile what information each main-table policy receives, making baseline fairness and the source of PvP's gains difficult to assess.

The claimed computational efficiency is not demonstrated quantitatively. Stating that training fits on one RTX 4090 does not establish minimal overhead; per-update time, total training time, memory, or FLOPs relative to PPO and other SRL methods are absent. Figure 16 alone also does not clearly show PvP as best in wall-clock time.

Methodological originality is limited: PvP is essentially SimSiam applied to a privileged state and its zero-masked view. There is no representation analysis or component ablation showing why this pairing works beyond simply exposing the shared encoder to privileged inputs, nor comparisons with simpler privileged-feature prediction or regularization alternatives.

Evaluation is largely reward-based and narrow relative to the robustness claims. The paper omits quantitative disturbance tests, domain-shift evaluation, sim-to-real gaps, energy or torque measurements, failure statistics, and held-out-motion generalization. Sim2Sim evaluation is likewise presented only through screenshots.

Several interpretations overreach the evidence. Faster optimization of an action-smoothness reward does not by itself “guarantee” deployment reliability, and the discussion attributes behavior to better task-relevant representations without directly evaluating representation quality or ruling out auxiliary-loss regularization effects.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details: motion-data provenance and splits, evaluation protocol, seed count, score normalization, stopping criteria, and exact real-robot setup are not sufficiently specified. Overall, the promising and potentially useful idea is outweighed by ambiguity in the core comparison and insufficient quantitative support for the main sample-efficiency and real-world claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving the sample efficiency of reinforcement-learning-based humanoid whole-body control. Using privileged simulator state only during training is operationally relevant because deployment still relies on proprioception.

PvP is simple and easy to integrate with an asymmetric actor-critic pipeline. The shared-encoder, stop-gradient objective adds limited architectural complexity and does not require a separately pretrained teacher.

The evaluation includes velocity tracking, motion imitation, rough-terrain locomotion, and a second humanoid platform. Comparisons against PPO, VAE, SPR, SimSiam, and teacher-student distillation provide broader evidence than a single-task study.

The manuscript reports useful implementation details, including observations, rewards, network architectures, PPO hyperparameters, and searches over auxiliary-loss settings. The update-frequency and data-proportion studies could offer practical guidance.

The learning curves consistently suggest that PvP can accelerate optimization, especially on the main velocity-tracking task. Sim-to-sim and real-robot demonstrations provide preliminary evidence that the learned policies are deployable.
weaknesses: The central technical interpretation is inadequately justified. Matching the representation of the full privileged state to that of its zero-masked version primarily encourages invariance to the privileged components; it is not evident why this transfers otherwise unavailable privileged information into the deployed representation. No probing, representation analysis, or controlled ablation demonstrates the claimed acquisition of task-relevant privileged features.

The method description contains a consequential dimensional inconsistency. Equation 2 defines the proprioceptive view by masking privileged components of s, while Section C.2 instead says that zeros are attached to the proprioceptive state to match the privileged-state dimension. Moreover, Table 2 uses five-frame proprioceptive histories but an apparently single-frame privileged state, so o is not straightforwardly a subset of s as assumed. This leaves the actual encoder inputs and masking operation insufficiently specified for reproduction.

The empirical reporting is too incomplete to support repeated claims of significant improvement. The number of random seeds is never stated, the meaning and normalization of the reported score are undefined, and there are no numerical tables, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or threshold-based sample-efficiency measurements. Shaded standard deviations alone do not establish significance.

The real-robot evidence is qualitative: the paper provides images and refers to videos but reports no number of trials, command distributions, tracking errors, success rates, disturbances, failure cases, or baseline comparisons on hardware. Consequently, claims of improved real-world reliability are not substantiated.

The computational-efficiency section gives no measured overhead, throughput, memory use, or training-time comparison, despite concluding that the framework has minimal computational cost. Iteration-based curves also do not measure sample efficiency completely because environment transitions and wall-clock costs are not consistently reported.

The novelty is limited. PvP is essentially a SimSiam-style consistency loss between a privileged input and a masked version, closely related to privileged-information distillation and modality-dropout ideas. The paper does not adequately distinguish its technical contribution from these established approaches, and calling SimSiam-style negative-free alignment 'contrastive learning' is imprecise.

Important controls are missing. The experiments do not isolate whether gains arise from privileged information, masking regularization, an additional encoder pass, loss scaling, or the particular hyperparameter selection. A direct privileged-variable prediction baseline, ordinary feature consistency without the predictor, random privileged-feature masking, and matched-compute controls would be especially informative.

Baseline tuning is potentially uneven: PvP's best coefficient is later reported as 0.1, whereas the main setting is stated to use 0.5, and the manuscript does not explain whether hyperparameters were selected independently per task or using held-out criteria. The teacher-student comparison also does not provide enough procedural detail to assess fairness.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Action smoothness is treated as sufficient evidence of real-world reliability, local optima are invoked without analysis, and 'task-relevant' representations are asserted without examining learned features or generalization. These are material scientific issues rather than presentation refinements.

The contribution to CVPR is weakly positioned: the method and experiments use low-dimensional robot states without visual perception, and the manuscript does not articulate a substantial computer-vision or pattern-recognition advance beyond generic representation learning. Overall, the promising empirical trend does not compensate for the ambiguity of the mechanism and insufficient quantitative validation.

strengths: PvP is a simple, practical way to exploit simulator-only information: a shared encoder aligns privileged and masked-proprioceptive views with a SimSiam-style objective while retaining a proprioception-only deployment path.

The empirical results are consistently favorable across velocity tracking and motion imitation. Additional rough-terrain and Unitree G1 experiments provide useful evidence that the gains are not confined to one task or robot configuration.
The paper studies several practically relevant design choices, including SRL update frequency, data proportion, encoder placement, loss weighting, and comparison with teacher-student distillation.

SRL4Humanoid could be a useful community contribution. The manuscript provides network, PPO, reward, observation, and baseline-search details, and reports that the code and training logs will be available.
The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and generally easy to follow.
weaknesses: The central quantitative evidence is underspecified. The normalized-score definition, number of random seeds, and normalization reference are not reported, while results are shown almost entirely as curves without numerical summaries, threshold-based sample-efficiency measurements, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. This makes the claimed significance and effect sizes difficult to assess.

The real-robot evidence is qualitative: photographs and a supporting video are cited, but there is no evaluation protocol, number of trials, success rate, tracking error, disturbance test, or comparison with PPO and other baselines. Consequently, claims about reliable real-world deployment are not adequately supported.

The methodological novelty is modest, essentially applying a SimSiam-style consistency loss to privileged and zero-masked observations. Comparisons do not isolate whether the benefit specifically comes from contrastive representation learning rather than simpler privileged-information prediction, feature matching, or regularization.

The representation-quality explanation remains speculative. There are no probing, latent-space, robustness, or generalization analyses demonstrating that PvP learns more task-relevant representations or filters noise and redundancy as claimed.

The state construction is not described consistently enough for exact reproduction. Section 3 assumes the proprioceptive state is a subset of the privileged state, but Tables 2 and 4 list differently sized and, for velocity tracking, differently stacked inputs; Appendix C only briefly mentions padding the proprioceptive input. The precise vectors passed to the shared encoder and policy should be formalized.

The computational-efficiency claim is not substantiated with measured training time, throughput, memory, or overhead for the main experiments; referring to externally attached logs is insufficient evidence in the manuscript itself.

The evaluation remains narrow for the broad claim of general SRL-empowered humanoid learning: most analyses use two tasks on one platform, all inputs are low-dimensional states, and there is no evaluation with visual perception despite the CVPR context. Overall, the promising and useful empirical contribution is balanced by insufficiently rigorous reporting and validation, placing the paper near the acceptance boundary.
